title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E420 recasts the calculus of variations by embedding the extremal curve AM, y = y(x), in a one-parameter family y(x,t). The variation of a quantity is its differential with respect to t; Euler writes it as dt(dy/dt), modern εη(x). For J = ∫Z dx with dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + S ds + …, where p = y', q = y'', and so on, §14 had found the variation δJ by repeated integration by parts.

The end of §36 (begun on p.56) gives a geometric model of the admissible neighbouring curves αμ:
- Draw an arbitrary curve BN over the axis AP.
- On each ordinate XYV, with Y on AM and V on BN, cut the segment YV at v so that Yv is an infinitesimal fraction of YV. In modern terms ỹ(x) = y(x) + εη(x), with η = YV and ε infinitesimal.
- On this page Euler adds a condition: BN must nowhere have a tangent perpendicular to the axis, i.e. η' must stay bounded, otherwise the division of the intervals would be disturbed.
- The consequence is that not only the gaps Yv but also the tangent directions at Y and v differ infinitesimally. In modern terms the varied curve is close in the C^1 sense: a weak variation.
- Together with §35 (no corners; the curves may be 'discontinuous', i.e. freehand, in Euler's sense), this states the admissible class.

§37 begins interpreting the §14 result. The first part of the variation is
 dt ∫ (dy/dt) [N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + d⁴S/dx⁴ − …] dx,
modern ε ∫_a^b η(x) E(x) dx, with E the Euler–Poisson expression. The integral is taken from A, the integration constant being fixed by vanishing at A. Geometrically, the elementary term at each point X is the vertical gap Yv = dt(dy/dt) weighted by E(x), and these terms are summed from A to M.

The next page draws the consequence: since the Yv are arbitrary in size and sign, this part vanishes for all neighbouring curves only if E ≡ 0, which is the Euler–Poisson equation. It then treats the boundary terms.
errors: No computational error on this page.

Conceptual gap: for integrands Z that depend on q = y'', r = y''', s = y'''', … (which the displayed formula with Q, R, S explicitly covers), closeness of the curves and their tangents is not enough. The varied curve must also stay close in the higher derivatives, so BN needs bounded higher derivatives as well. Euler states only the first-order conditions: no corners (§35) and no vertical tangents.
Implicitly the base curve AM must also avoid vertical tangents and singularities. This is not stated.

ideas.what: Neighbouring curves built as y + ε·(arbitrary curve BN − y), with ε infinitesimal
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (δ-method, 1755/1760), with Euler's t-parameter reformulation in E420

ideas.what: Requirement that the arbitrary curve have no vertical tangent, so that the varied curve's tangents differ infinitesimally from those of AM
ideas.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass (lectures from 1879) for the explicit weak/strong distinction; Legendre and Jacobi implicitly
ideas.where_published: This page; Euler's other papers on variations, unsure

ideas.modern_name: Admissible class of C^1 comparison functions, not necessarily analytic
ideas.where_published: E420 §35; related to Euler's position in the vibrating-string controversy

ideas.what: First part of the variation as ε∫η·E dx with E the Euler–Poisson expression, interpreted pointwise via the gaps Yv

missed.claim: Euler explicitly restricts neighbouring curves so that tangents are also infinitesimally close, an early explicit statement of weak (C^1) variations a century before Weierstrass's weak/strong distinction. Historians such as Goldstine and Fraser discuss E420, so this is likely at least partly noticed. It may deserve a sharper credit as a precursor remark.
missed.quote: non solum interualla Yv esse infinite parva, sed etiam tangentes in punctis Y et v infinite parum a parallelismo deficere
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: History of the notion of the topology on the admissible class (weak vs strong extrema). It is a minor attribution nuance, not new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The C^1-closeness remark is a nice explicit precursor of weak variations, but it follows naturally from Euler's one-parameter framework. E420 is well studied, so the remark is probably known to historians of the calculus of variations.
transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially accurate. 'Y v' should read 'Yv' (Y and lowercase italic v). The footer '38.' is the catchword for the next section.
